title: Federal procurement: Acquisition speed can weaken accountability
desc: Centers continuing use-case evaluation, enforceable vendor evidence, full operating costs and lock-in avoidance.

kps.k: Federal AI governance centres on accountable procurement and continuing evaluation, rather than adoption or benchmark performance alone.
kps.d: OMB’s M-25-22 couples faster, competitive acquisition with measurable mission outcomes and lifecycle safeguards. The Law of Evaluation argues that agencies should connect AI testing to established administrative-law, evidence-building and procurement obligations. GAO supplies case-based evidence of implementation problems, not proof of which procurement approach works best: its October 2024–April 2026 audit reviewed 13 acquisitions at DOD, DHS, GSA and VA, alongside Commerce initiatives, using a nongeneralizable sample. The sources largely agree on the governance objective; their differences concern implementation, enforceability and capacity. Efficiency gains remain policy ambitions or attributed claims rather than established comparative results.

qs.q: In carrying out this direction, agencies must procure effective and trustworthy AI capabilities in a timely and cost-effective manner.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: By situating AI evaluation within the wider landscape of federal performance measurement, evidence-based policymaking, and procurement quality assurance, we argue that effective AI governance requires reconnecting the emerging AI toolkit with longstanding evaluation obligations in administrative and procurement law.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Accelerating acquisition can sacrifice the contractual protections needed to manage AI after deployment.
kps.d: GAO contrasts slower agency-directed procurement, which permits tailored requirements, with faster vendor-driven upgrades that may omit safeguards against cost growth and declining reliability. FEMA officials reported that using an existing contract accelerated acquisition but prevented them from requiring post-award testing. OMB seeks to reconcile speed and control through cross-functional planning, outcome-based specifications and risk-proportionate effort. GAO describes service procurement as often preferable because AI requires continuing assessment, but does not establish a universal preference or a winning procurement vehicle.

qs.q: The benefits of an agency-directed approach using typical acquisition planning steps include a deliberate decision-making process that involves AI terms and conditions that reflect agency requirements.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: However, not including AI terms and conditions when using this approach may increase the risk of experiencing unanticipated cost growth and operational challenges, such as “model drift”— decreasing reliability over time.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Evaluation must establish fitness for the actual use case and continue as systems, prices and conditions change.
kps.d: OMB requires pre-award testing to the greatest extent practicable and contractual access for ongoing evaluation. Independent evaluations must use agency-defined data; those data should resemble deployment data and remain unavailable to vendors. The Law of Evaluation argues that benchmarks, red-teaming and pilots alone often miss deployment-relevant questions. GAO reports that NIST officials see no well-defined universal tests, while GSA’s USAi team tests models over time to assess performance and whether upgrades justify higher prices. Practical measures include mission-linked baselines, performance standards for new versions, rollback provisions and periodic decisions about continued use—not a one-time approval.

qs.q: Part I diagnoses why prevailing approaches to AI evaluation—benchmarking, internal pilots, red-teaming, impact assessments, and periodic audits—regularly fail to answer the questions that matter in real deployments, even as executive- branch guidance has begun to push agencies toward more systematic testing and monitoring.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Agencies must use data they have defined (e.g., agency validation and          testing datasets) when conducting any independent evaluations to ensure the          AI system or service is fit for purpose.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Vendor accountability depends on enforceable access, data rights and evidence obligations, not assurances alone.
kps.d: OMB requires clear government–contractor ownership terms, monitoring access and internal visibility into vendor testing. It permits vendor-conducted testing when appropriate, subject to close agency monitoring and reproducibility safeguards where practicable. GAO illustrates the consequences of weak terms: FEMA could not share outputs with partners, and Maven officials could not enforce weekly deliverables until they clarified requirements. The Law of Evaluation reads existing procurement law as placing evidentiary responsibilities on vendors, but proposes further reform: explicitly invalidate no-testing and no-benchmarking clauses in rights- and safety-impacting contracts and clarify safeguarded disclosure to retained independent evaluators. These proposals go beyond the explicit protections described in current OMB guidance.

qs.q: Contracts must detail the examination, testing, and validation procedures of          the vendor and must not prohibit agencies from internally disclosing how          the vendor conducts testing or the results of testing.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Thus, FAR puts the burden of proof on AI vendors, instead of the purchasing agency – an important distinction given agencies’ resourcing constraints.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Long-term value requires avoiding lock-in and assessing full operating costs, including the option to stop using a system.
kps.d: OMB recommends portability, interoperability, knowledge transfer and transparent licensing from solicitation through closeout. GAO reports difficulties understanding pricing and sustaining infrastructure. Army officials rejected an XM-30 proposal of roughly $300,000 per vehicle annually, which would have exceeded $500 million a year in licensing alone; these were proposed costs, not expenditure. VA officials retired SoKAT in January 2023 because its incremental benefits did not justify its cost. Together, these accounts support attention to total lifecycle costs, transition rights and sunset criteria, without demonstrating savings from any particular pricing model.

qs.q: As agencies seek to accelerate the adoption of AI-enabled services, they must pay careful attention to vendor sourcing, data portability, and long-term interoperability4 to avoid significant and costly dependencies on a single vendor.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: For example, officials from the Army’s XM-30 AI solution, which provides enhanced targeting for its minimally crewed infantry combat vehicles, stated that AI licensing fees can be exorbitant, citing proposals that included prices for around $300,000 per vehicle per year.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Rights protections persist alongside adoption policies, but policy scope and evaluative criteria remain important limits.
kps.d: The ABA Year 1 report describes earlier design principles, independent testing and NIST risk-management institutions; these are reported government measures, not independent ABA findings. The Law of Evaluation identifies substantial continuity in testing, impact assessment and monitoring across administrations despite the shift to a high-impact AI category. The Year 2 report describes additional human oversight and agency governance requirements, while questioning how procurement neutrality can operate without defined objectivity criteria. M-25-22 is not a blanket rule for every federal or private AI use: it excludes Intelligence Community elements, National Security System components and specified other uses, and phases in contract coverage after 180 days.

qs.q: [4] The blueprint also described design principles that would support these goals: careful design from the outset of system development; public oversight; independent testing and reporting; and personalization to the individual (in terms of data collected, control of that data, and explanations given).
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Agencies must only procure AI models that are “objective and free from top-down ideological bias.” The criteria for assessing “objectivity” have not been defined and ensuring neutrality in AI systems under the “preventing woke” executive order will be challenging.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Institutional capacity and systematic learning determine whether formal safeguards become operational.
kps.d: OMB calls for multidisciplinary teams and shared procurement resources, but GAO reports shortages of technical expertise and finds that DOD, DHS, GSA and VA policies effective as of September 2025 lacked systematic requirements to document acquisition lessons. Missing records included SoKAT’s retirement and FEMA’s model limitations. GAO recommends mandatory collection and sharing; agency concurrence does not establish implementation. The Law of Evaluation similarly finds limited use of Evidence Act planning for AI and advocates shared evaluation capacity, while noting that its proposed institutional template, GSA’s Office of Evaluation Sciences, no longer exists. The practical implication is to fund expertise and embed documentation, reusable contract terms and feedback into ordinary acquisition processes rather than rely on guidance or repositories alone.

qs.q: **Access to subject matter experts.** Officials from each of our five selected agencies told us that limited access to subject matter experts, such as data scientists and software engineers, was a challenge for procuring AI technologies.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: 81 The disappointing lack of evaluation of AI use cases suggests that the Evidence Act’s most promising tools—learning agendas and coordinated evaluation plans—have, so far, done little to structure AI evaluation.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academic source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that federal AI procurement requires continuing, use-case-specific evaluation and enforceable vendor accountability rather than reliance on acquisition speed or benchmark performance alone. It materially extends that proposition by locating these safeguards in existing administrative-law, Evidence Act and procurement-quality-assurance obligations, including an evidentiary burden on vendors. It also proposes concrete legal reinforcement: making contractual prohibitions on testing or benchmarking unenforceable and preserving access for independent evaluators. Its qualifications concern implementation rather than direction: current evaluation practices remain incomplete, agency planning and expertise are underdeveloped, and the cited shared-capacity model no longer exists. The source concentrates less on the cluster’s separate concerns about total operating costs and vendor lock-in, so its contribution is strongest on evaluation, enforceability and institutional capacity.

qs.q: By situating AI evaluation within the wider landscape of federal performance measurement, evidence-based policymaking, and procurement quality assurance, we argue that effective AI governance requires reconnecting the emerging AI toolkit with longstanding evaluation obligations in administrative and procurement law.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Congress and OMB could make explicit that “no testing” or “no benchmarking” clauses in rights- and safety-impacting AI contracts are contrary to public policy and unenforceable, much as certain indemnification and nondisclosure terms already are.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: Across this curated set of regulators, oversight bodies and professional-body reports, the professional voice accepts the proposition that acquisition speed must not displace accountability and materially develops it into an operational governance framework. The common rationale is that AI performance, risks, prices and vendor offerings change after award, so agencies need use-case-specific testing, enforceable monitoring access, data and IP rights, portability, transparent lifecycle costs, human oversight and the ability to discontinue systems. GAO adds case-based evidence that expedient contracting can prevent post-award testing and that weak expertise, requirements and documentation impair vendor accountability; it further extends the proposition through a concrete recommendation for systematic collection and sharing of acquisition lessons. Material variation concerns evidentiary strength and scope: OMB prescribes safeguards but does not prove their effectiveness; GAO documents implementation failures in a nongeneralizable set of acquisitions and says it is too early to identify a superior procurement approach; the ABA Year 2 report supports continuing risk controls while addressing procurement accountability less specifically; and the ABA Year 1 report only surveys broad governance principles, leaving its position on the speed–accountability trade-off unclear. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: As agencies seek to accelerate the adoption of AI-enabled services, they must pay careful attention to vendor sourcing, data portability, and long-term interoperability4 to avoid significant and costly dependencies on a single vendor.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The August 2024 source is broadly compatible with the proposition’s accountability objective: it reports federal principles favouring careful design, public oversight, independent testing, and institutional attention to AI risk. However, this is background description of government frameworks and advisory institutions, not procurement-specific evidence or argument. It does not assess whether acquisition speed weakens contractual safeguards, nor does it address continuing use-case evaluation, enforceable vendor evidence, lifecycle costs, data rights, or lock-in. Internal variation is limited to different governance mechanisms—design principles, NIST risk work, federally supported research, and interdisciplinary advice—none of which establishes a position on the proposition as framed. Because this time period contains only one curated source, no broader prevalence inference is warranted.

qs.q: [4] The blueprint also described design principles that would support these goals: careful design from the outset of system development; public oversight; independent testing and reporting; and personalization to the individual (in terms of data collected, control of that data, and explanations given).
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: Across these selected 2025 sources, accelerated federal AI adoption is accepted as a policy objective, but only alongside procurement and governance controls that preserve accountability after deployment. M-25-22 provides the most direct and operational support: it links faster acquisition to realistic use-case testing, enforceable monitoring access, vendor-testing evidence, data portability, interoperability, lifecycle-cost assessment and sunset criteria. The Year 2 report supports the same core position at a broader governance level, pairing the removal of procurement barriers with pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, ongoing monitoring and human oversight for high-impact AI. Material variation lies in specificity and evidentiary status: M-25-22 establishes detailed requirements and recommendations, while the report mainly describes federal policy and flags undefined model-objectivity criteria. Neither source supplies comparative evidence that faster adoption produces efficiency gains or that the safeguards are effective in practice.

qs.q: As agencies seek to accelerate the adoption of AI-enabled services, they must pay careful attention to vendor sourcing, data portability, and long-term interoperability4 to avoid significant and costly dependencies on a single vendor.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the proposition that faster federal AI acquisition can weaken accountability unless procurement embeds use-case-specific, continuing evaluation, enforceable vendor obligations, lifecycle-cost scrutiny and institutional learning. They materially develop it in complementary ways. The Law of Evaluation supplies the legal architecture, tying AI oversight to administrative law, the Evidence Act and procurement quality assurance, placing evidentiary responsibility on vendors and proposing that contractual barriers to testing and independent evaluation be made unenforceable. GAO adds case-based implementation evidence: expedited contracting can prevent post-award testing, while weak data rights, unclear performance requirements, limited expertise, opaque costs and failures to document lessons impede lifecycle control. GAO further recommends systematic collection and sharing of acquisition lessons. Material variation concerns emphasis and certainty rather than direction: the legal analysis advances stronger rules and institutional models, whereas GAO focuses on operational shortcomings and cautions that its 13-acquisition, nongeneralizable review cannot establish which procurement model or initiative performs best. Both therefore support the proposition while extending it from a general speed–accountability trade-off into concrete legal, contractual and organisational reforms.
